Each primary laser light beam is coupled into a first end of the respective light guide and coupled out of a second end of the light guide as a secondary laser light beam. outputs.L2: The invention concerns a vehicle laser illumination apparatus that includes at least two laser light sources. Each laser light source is arranged to produce a primary laser beam and is assigned a corresponding light guide. The primary laser beam from each source is introduced into a first end of the respective light guide and exits from a second end of that guide as a secondary laser beam. Each secondary laser beam is then aimed at a light conversion element to create a predetermined light pattern on it. outputs.L3:
The invention relates to a laser-based lighting device for vehicles, in particular for generating a predefined light distribution on a roadway in front of the vehicle. The device comprises two or more laser light sources, each of which is configured to emit a primary laser light beam.

Each laser light source is optically coupled to an associated light guide. The primary laser light beam generated by a respective laser light source is coupled into the corresponding light guide and subsequently coupled out again. During propagation through the light guide, the primary laser light beam is transformed such that, after exiting the light guide, it forms a secondary laser light beam having an intensity profile different from that of the original primary laser light beam. In this way, the beam characteristics of each laser light source can be adapted before further optical processing.

The secondary laser light beams are then directed onto a light conversion means by means of a microscanner. The microscanner deflects or scans the secondary laser light beams in a controlled manner so that they impinge on the light conversion means at predetermined positions and in a predetermined sequence. As a result, a defined luminous image is produced on or in the light conversion means.

The light conversion means may convert at least part of the incident laser radiation into visible light suitable for vehicle illumination. By controlling the laser light sources and the microscanner, the luminous image can be generated with a desired shape, brightness distribution, and spatial resolution.

A projection system is arranged downstream of the light conversion means. This projection system projects the luminous image generated by the light conversion means onto the roadway, thereby producing a desired illumination pattern in front of the vehicle. The use of multiple laser light sources, associated light guides, and controlled scanning enables a flexible and efficient vehicle lighting device capable of forming predefined light distributions with high precision.
outputs.L4:
A vehicle laser lighting device is designed to generate a controlled light distribution, such as a roadway projection or an adaptive headlamp image, by using a plurality of laser light sources. Each laser source emits a primary laser beam, and each primary beam is directed into a corresponding light guide. The light guides are arranged to modify the intensity profile of the respective laser beams before the beams are further processed. In particular, the light guides may reshape, homogenize, widen, narrow, or otherwise adjust the spatial distribution of the laser radiation so that each beam has a desired intensity characteristic when it reaches the next optical stage.

After passing through the light guides, the primary laser beams are directed toward corresponding microscanners. The microscanners deflect the beams in a controlled manner and scan them over a light conversion element. The light conversion element may include a phosphor or another wavelength-converting material that converts the primary laser radiation into secondary light. For example, blue or ultraviolet laser radiation may be converted into white, yellow, or another visible light suitable for vehicle illumination.

The secondary beams produced by the light conversion element are then collected and shaped by a projection system. The projection system projects the generated light outward from the vehicle to form a predefined luminous image on the roadway or in the vehicle’s forward field of view. This image may correspond to a low-beam distribution, high-beam distribution, glare-free high-beam pattern, marking light, warning symbol, lane guidance indication, or another adaptive illumination pattern.

By changing the intensity profiles of the laser beams before scanning, the device allows the luminous image to be generated with improved precision and flexibility. The use of individual light guides for the respective laser sources enables better control over brightness distribution, edge sharpness, and local illumination intensity. As a result, the lighting device can produce complex and adaptable light patterns while maintaining efficient use of laser light. This makes the system particularly suitable for modern vehicle lighting applications in which illumination must be dynamically adjusted according to driving conditions, road geometry, traffic participants, and driver assistance functions.
outputs.L5:
**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the most common words in the English language, but it is also one of the most important. Although it is short and simple, it plays a major role in helping us understand meaning. The word “the” is called a definite article, which means it points to something specific.

For example, when we say “a book,” we could mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we are talking about a particular book that the speaker and listener both know about. This small word helps make communication clearer and more precise.

“The” is used before nouns to show that something is already known, unique, or clearly identified. We say “the sun” because there is only one sun in our sky. We say “the teacher” when we know which teacher is being discussed. In this way, “the” helps connect ideas and gives context to a sentence.

Even though it may seem ordinary, “the” is essential in everyday English. Without it, sentences can sound unnatural or unclear. This tiny word shows that even the smallest parts of language can have great importance.

counterfactuals.output:
A vehicle lighting system is provided for generating a predefined luminous image, such as a headlamp beam distribution, signaling pattern, symbol, or adaptive lighting graphic. The system comprises at least two laser light sources, each configured to emit a respective primary light beam. Each laser light source is optically coupled to an associated light guide arranged to receive and guide the respective primary light beam toward an output region.

The light guides are configured to emit respective secondary light beams derived from the primary light beams. Each secondary light beam is directed toward a corresponding microscanner or scanning element. The microscanners are operable to deflect the secondary light beams in a controlled manner, for example in one or more scanning directions, so as to generate scanned light distributions. A projection system is arranged downstream of the microscanners and is configured to project the scanned light distributions outwardly from the vehicle lighting system.

The laser light sources, light guides, microscanners, and projection system are arranged and controlled such that the secondary light beams are combined or coordinated to form the predefined luminous image in a target projection region. The predefined luminous image may be generated by spatial and/or temporal modulation of the laser light sources and by synchronized actuation of the microscanners. The use of multiple laser light sources and associated optical paths enables increased brightness, improved image resolution, redundancy, and flexible formation of static or dynamic light patterns suitable for vehicle exterior lighting functions.

In some embodiments, the system includes a controller configured to control the intensity, timing, wavelength, and/or modulation of the laser light sources and the scanning behavior of the microscanners. The controller may adapt the projected luminous image in response to vehicle operating conditions, sensor data, road geometry, traffic participants, or driver inputs. The projection system may include one or more lenses, mirrors, collimating optics, combining optics, or imaging optics to shape and direct the scanned beams into the desired luminous distribution.

The invention thereby provides a compact and adaptable laser-based vehicle lighting system capable of producing high-definition luminous images with precise spatial control, suitable for applications including adaptive driving beams, glare-free high beam functions, road marking projections, warning symbols, turn indication, communication lighting, and other vehicle illumination or signaling features.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a European patent application-style description of a laser lighting device for vehicles in which each laser beam passes through a guide, changes intensity profile, and is directed onto a conversion surface before roadway projection.
counterfactuals.output:
**Description**

**Laser Lighting Device for a Motor Vehicle**

The invention relates to a lighting device for a motor vehicle, in particular to a headlamp or auxiliary lighting module configured to generate a light distribution on a roadway by means of laser radiation converted into visible illumination.

Conventional vehicle lighting devices increasingly employ laser light sources because of their high luminance and compact construction. In many arrangements, a laser beam is directed onto a wavelength conversion element, for example a phosphor surface, which converts at least part of the laser radiation into visible light. The converted light is then imaged or projected by an optical system onto the roadway in front of the vehicle.

However, a laser beam generally has a highly concentrated and often substantially Gaussian intensity profile. If such a beam is directed directly onto a conversion surface, the resulting excitation spot may exhibit excessive peak intensity, local heating, non-uniform conversion, and a limited useful light distribution. It is therefore desirable to modify the intensity profile of the laser beam before it reaches the conversion surface, while maintaining compactness and optical efficiency.

According to the present disclosure, a laser lighting device is provided in which each laser beam emitted by a laser light source passes through a respective optical guide. During propagation through the guide, the beam is shaped such that its intensity profile is changed. The beam emerging from the guide is then directed onto a conversion surface. The conversion surface emits converted light, which is subsequently projected onto a roadway by a projection optical system.

In this manner, a laser beam having an initially narrow or peaked intensity distribution may be transformed into a widened, homogenised, rectangular, strip-like, annular, or otherwise predetermined intensity profile before it impinges on the conversion surface. The converted light emitted from the conversion surface may therefore have improved uniformity and may be better adapted to the desired vehicle light distribution.

An exemplary embodiment will now be described with reference to the figures, which are schematic only.

**Fig. 1** shows a schematic side view of a laser lighting device.

**Fig. 2** shows a schematic front view of a conversion surface illuminated by a plurality of shaped laser beams.

**Fig. 3** shows an exemplary guide for changing the intensity profile of a laser beam.

A laser lighting device 1 comprises a housing 2 configured for installation in a motor vehicle, for example in a front headlamp. The lighting device 1 comprises a plurality of laser light sources 3. Each laser light source 3 may be a semiconductor laser diode configured to emit a laser beam 4. The laser light sources 3 may emit blue or violet laser radiation, for example radiation having a wavelength suitable for exciting a wavelength conversion material.

Each laser beam 4 emitted by a corresponding laser light source 3 is coupled into a respective guide 5. The guide 5 may be an optical waveguide, light pipe, rod integrator, hollow reflective guide, solid transparent guide, fibre guide, or another optical element configured to conduct the laser beam 4 from an input region 6 to an output region 7.

The guide 5 is configured such that, while the laser beam 4 propagates through the guide 5, the intensity profile of the beam is changed. In particular, the guide 5 may transform an input intensity profile, for example a substantially Gaussian profile or an elliptical profile, into an output intensity profile having a predetermined shape. The output intensity profile may be more uniform than the input intensity profile. Alternatively or additionally, the output intensity profile may be widened, flattened, elongated, split, or otherwise redistributed.

The change of intensity profile may be produced by one or more of internal reflections, total internal reflection, diffuse reflection, refractive shaping, scattering, mode mixing, or geometrical transformation within the guide 5. The guide 5 may have a non-circular cross-section, for example a rectangular, square, polygonal, elliptical, or segment-shaped cross-section. In one embodiment, the guide 5 is a rod integrator having a rectangular cross-section, so that the laser beam 4 is mixed by multiple internal reflections and emerges with a substantially rectangular intensity distribution.

The guide 5 may also have a varying cross-section along its length. For example, the guide 5 may comprise a tapering portion 8, a widening portion, a curved portion, or a stepped portion. Such a configuration may alter the angular distribution and spatial distribution of the laser radiation. The guide 5 may further comprise an input optical surface adapted to couple the laser beam 4 into the guide 5 and an output optical surface adapted to emit the shaped laser beam 9 toward a conversion surface 10.

The shaped laser beam 9 emerging from the output region 7 of the guide 5 is directed onto the conversion surface 10. The conversion surface 10 comprises a wavelength conversion material, for example a phosphor, ceramic phosphor, phosphor layer, phosphor plate, or luminescent conversion element. The conversion surface 10 is configured to absorb at least part of the laser radiation and to emit converted light 11 having a wavelength different from the wavelength of the laser radiation. In particular, blue laser radiation may excite a yellow-emitting phosphor, so that a mixture of remaining blue light and converted yellow light forms white light.

The conversion surface 10 may be arranged on a carrier 12. The carrier 12 may be thermally conductive and may be connected to a heat sink 13 in order to dissipate heat generated during conversion. The conversion surface 10 may be operated in reflection, wherein converted light 11 is emitted generally toward a projection optical system 14 on the same side from which the laser radiation is incident. Alternatively, the conversion surface 10 may be operated in transmission.

The projection optical system 14 is arranged downstream of the conversion surface 10 in the optical path of the converted light 11. The projection optical system 14 may comprise one or more lenses, reflectors, collimators, projection lenses, or free-form optical elements. The projection optical system 14 projects the light emitted by the conversion surface 10 onto a roadway 15 in front of the vehicle, thereby forming a light distribution 16. The light distribution 16 may be a low-beam distribution, a high-beam distribution, a partial high-beam distribution, a cornering light distribution, a marking light distribution, or an adaptive driving beam distribution.

In the embodiment shown schematically in Fig. 2, a plurality of shaped laser beams 9a, 9b, 9c are directed onto different regions of the conversion surface 10. Each of the laser beams 9a, 9b, 9c has passed through a corresponding guide 5a, 5b, 5c before reaching the conversion surface 10. The guides 5a, 5b, 5c may be configured differently from one another, such that the shaped laser beams 9a, 9b, 9c have different intensity profiles, spot sizes, or spot shapes on the conversion surface 10.

For example, a first guide 5a may generate a horizontally elongated excitation region for producing a wide basic illumination region of the roadway. A second guide 5b may generate a more concentrated excitation region for producing a high-intensity central region. A third guide 5c may generate an asymmetric excitation region for producing a cut-off region or shoulder illumination region. By controlling the laser light sources 3 individually, the lighting device 1 may generate an adaptive light distribution.

The direction of each shaped laser beam 9 onto the conversion surface 10 may be determined by the orientation of the guide 5, by a coupling optic, by an output surface of the guide, or by an additional deflecting element 17. The deflecting element 17 may comprise a mirror, prism, lens, diffractive element, or free-form optical element. In one embodiment, the output surface of the guide 5 is inclined relative to the longitudinal axis of the guide, so that the shaped laser beam 9 is emitted at a predetermined angle toward the conversion surface 10.

The guide 5 may be formed from glass, quartz, sapphire, transparent ceramic, polymer material, or another material transparent to the wavelength of the laser radiation. In a hollow guide embodiment, internal surfaces may be provided with reflective coatings. In a solid guide embodiment, the refractive index and boundary surfaces may be selected to provide total internal reflection.

The guide 5 may additionally perform a safety function. Since the laser radiation is enclosed within the guide 5 over at least part of its propagation path, stray laser radiation inside the lighting device 1 may be reduced. The guide 5 may also be fixed relative to the conversion surface 10, thereby maintaining stable illumination of the conversion surface 10 even under vibration of the motor vehicle.

The intensity profile transformation provided by the guide 5 may reduce local peak intensities on the conversion surface 10. This may improve thermal behaviour, reduce degradation of the conversion material, and provide a more homogeneous luminance distribution. Furthermore, because the shape of the excitation region on the conversion surface 10 can be predetermined by the guide 5, the subsequent projection of the converted light can be adapted more efficiently to the desired roadway illumination.

In one embodiment, the guide 5 changes the laser beam 4 from a substantially Gaussian input profile into a top-hat output profile. In another embodiment, the guide 5 changes an elliptic laser beam profile into a substantially rectangular output profile. In a further embodiment, the guide 5 produces an output profile having a brightness gradient, for example a higher intensity in one region and a lower intensity in another region, in order to generate a desired gradient in the projected roadway light distribution.

The laser light sources 3 may be controlled by a control unit 18. The control unit 18 may adjust the power of each laser light source 3 independently. The control unit 18 may also switch individual laser light sources 3 on and off to vary the illumination pattern on the conversion surface 10 and therefore the light distribution 16 projected onto the roadway 15. Sensor signals, vehicle speed, steering angle, navigation data, camera data, or detected traffic participants may be taken into account for adaptive control.

The lighting device 1 may further comprise a monitoring sensor 19 configured to detect light emitted from the conversion surface 10 or scattered laser radiation. The monitoring sensor 19 may be connected to the control unit 18, which may reduce or interrupt laser operation if an abnormal operating condition is detected, for example damage to the conversion surface 10, misalignment of a guide 5, or excessive laser leakage.

Although the described embodiments refer primarily to a front headlamp, the lighting device may also be used in other vehicle lighting applications, including auxiliary driving lamps, fog lamps, signal lamps, projection lamps, or road marking systems.

The disclosed device therefore provides a compact and efficient vehicle lighting arrangement in which each laser beam is guided, reshaped in intensity profile, and directed onto a conversion surface prior to projection onto the roadway. This enables controlled illumination of the conversion surface, improved uniformity, reduced thermal loading, and flexible generation of vehicle light distributions.
